```{r}
library(readxl)
library(ggplot2)

sleep_data <- read_excel("Project Sleep Data.xlsx")
sleep_data1 <- subset(sleep_data, `Audio Type` != "NULL" & Day != 15)
sleep_data1$`Hours Slept` <- as.numeric(sleep_data1$`Hours Slept`)
head(sleep_data)
```
## Data Analysis

The current data analysis includes 20 nights of sleep observations across four audio categories. The results showed that calming music had the highest average sleep duration at 7.54 hours, while no audio had the lowest at 6.60 hours. Audiobook/ASMR had the highest average perceived sleep quality at 7.4 out of 10, compared to 6.4 for no audio. No audio also had the highest average number of disturbances at 4.6 per night.

An interesting effect that came from listening to audio while asleep was the effect it had on restless sleep duration. Using a sleep tracking app that used microphone recordings to track sleep movement; I was able to estimate just about how long I was remaining awake throughout the night while trying to sleep. Restless duration was estimated each morning based on the disturbances tracked in the app and what I remembered from the night before. Waking moments were considered a larger disturbance and accounted for a longer duration of time to account for falling back to sleep, and smaller disturbances in which I didn't remember waking up which were recorded by the app were treated as shorter durations. I estimated each night how long I was restless during each waking disturbance and recorded the average in minutes. Because these were self estimates rather than device measurements keeping track of when i fell back to sleep they are approximate. Throughout the period of analysis this seemed like a less tangible statistic due to the estimation and uncertainty, but it didn't make sense to not continue when I already had what I thought was a good system for recording it. 

When all three audio types are compared to no audio. No audio nights had a significantly higher sleep quality. This could suggest that having some sort of audio helps compared to none, and almost makes me feel like I should inlcude some sort of T-test to compare audio versus no audio but the number of nights would be slightly scewed to nights in which I had audio playing. 


```{r}
ggplot(data = sleep_data1,
       aes(x = Day, y = `Hours Slept`, color = `Audio Type`)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(x = "Day", y = "Hours Slept", color = "Audio Type") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:21) +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 16))
```

```{r}
ggplot(data = sleep_data1,
       aes(x = `Audio Type`, y = `Hours Slept`)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue", color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Audio Type", y = "Hours Slept") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 16))
```

```{r}
ggplot(data = sleep_data1,
       aes(x = as.numeric(`Quality (1–10)`), fill = `Audio Type`)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, boundary = 0.5,
                 position = "dodge", color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Sleep Quality Rating (1–10)", y = "Frequency", fill = "Audio Type") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 16))
```

## Anova results
### Sleep Quality Rating
```{r}
quality_anova <- aov(as.numeric(`Quality (1–10)`) ~ `Audio Type`,
                    data = sleep_data1)

summary(quality_anova)
```

### Sleep duration.
```{r}
hours_anova <- aov(as.numeric(`Hours Slept`) ~ `Audio Type`,
                   data = sleep_data1)

summary(hours_anova)
```
